insight.title: Free Bets Raise Your Risk Limit
insight.subtitle: Promos don't just lure you in—they reset what a normal bet feels like.
insight.notificationHook: Free bets quietly raise your risk limit

sections.text: Betting apps constantly offer "risk-free" promos and bonus credits. It looks like aggressive marketing, but the company isn't actually trying to win back that promotional money on your first wager.
Placing a free fifty-dollar bet recalibrates your baseline. Once you get used to the rush of a large payout, your normal five-dollar wagers suddenly feel too small to be exciting.
When the free credits run out, you keep betting at the elevated amount using your own bank account. The casino willingly loses a small bonus to permanently upgrade your risk tolerance.
Free money isn't a gift; it's a recalibration.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's news.

Democrats won control of both the United States Senate and House of Representatives on November fourth. Global stock markets rose after initially falling. President Donald Trump has two years remaining in his term. Trump said he will act as Mr Veto to block Democratic laws. Economist Stephen Brown at Capital Economics said the election changes little for near-term policy. Fellow Jacob Funk Kirkegaard at the Peterson Institute said Washington faces two years of gridlock. Voter opposition to artificial intelligence data centers helped several Democrats win their elections. A Pew Research Center poll showed fifty-six percent of Americans view Trump's tariff policies negatively. Congress can now take legal action against tariffs to prevent further trade escalation.

Next, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Democratic midterm victories could bring more United States help for Ukraine. Zelenskyy spoke to German broadcaster ZDF on Wednesday. He said Democrats speak clearly about supporting Ukraine and renewing ties with Europe. European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas urged Congress to increase pressure on Russia. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz doubted President Trump would change how he governs. Last month, Trump waived sanctions on Russia that Congress had previously approved. Trump envoy Steve Witkoff said peace talks will happen in Abu Dhabi on November tenth and eleventh. Zelenskyy wrote on X that Ukraine is ready to take necessary steps for peace.

Turning to technology news. Shares of major technology companies rose on Wednesday after election results removed market uncertainty. Amazon stock surged eight percent, and Google rose over six percent. Apple climbed nearly seven percent after recently receiving tariff refunds. Voters rejected artificial intelligence data centers in forty out of forty-one local ballot measures on Tuesday. Tesla stock fell two percent, and SpaceX dropped three percent. Nvidia, the company that makes most AI chips, slipped just over one percent. Smaller cloud provider CoreWeave saw its stock fall ten percent. Analyst Laura Martin at Needham said major incumbents will benefit from higher regulatory barriers. Axe Compute chief executive Chris Miglino said companies are still actively raising capital for data capacity.

In healthcare business, CVS Health announced plans to split its pharmacy chain from its health insurance operations. CVS Health is a healthcare company valued at one hundred seventeen billion dollars. The firm will split nine thousand retail pharmacies and mail-order services into CVS Pharmacy. A second company will keep insurer Aetna and pharmacy manager Caremark under the name CVS Health. CVS Health generated over four hundred billion dollars in revenue last year. Arkansas and Tennessee passed laws to stop health companies from managing both prescriptions and retail stores. Chief executive David Joyner will run the healthcare solutions business. The official breakup of CVS Health is scheduled for early 2028.

Next, American voters rejected local artificial intelligence projects despite arguments about competing with China. Midterm voters expressed strong concerns over rising power bills and heavy water usage from data centers. Brookings Institution fellow Kyle Chan said competing with China in AI no longer sways voters. Asia Society Policy Institute fellow Lizzi Lee said using China to justify tech spending is less effective. Gubernatorial candidates who proposed data center moratoriums won elections in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio. A poll showed fifty-six percent of voters considered data centers a major factor in their vote. Local voters ultimately voted against data centers in forty out of forty-one ballot measures across the country.

Turning to world news. India is monitoring how the United States midterm election results affect trade and immigration policy. Democratic majorities will take control of both houses of the US Congress in January. Nearly ten million Indian citizens live in West Asia, where war has disrupted energy imports. Dragonfly analyst Eddie Bejarano said Democrats could add language to spending bills blocking military funds. President Trump waived sanctions on major buyers of Russian energy on October sixteenth. Government figures show Indians received seventy-one percent of approved H-1B skilled work visas in recent years. A federal judge ruled in June that Trump's one hundred thousand dollar H-1B fee was unauthorized.

Next, typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes the Pacific burn with fever.

Severe typhoons boosted by the El Nino weather pattern have struck East Asia over recent months. El Nino is a natural climate event where warm ocean waters trigger extreme weather globally. The United Kingdom Met Office forecasts this El Nino will last until February or March. Typhoon Champi skirted Taiwan with winds reaching 295 kilometers per hour. The storm forced flight cancellations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Japan. It also cut electricity to 15,000 homes in Japan's Okinawa islands. Equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures rose 4 degrees Celsius above normal last month. That is the highest level recorded since 1949. Climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino found warmer temperatures increased storm rainfall by 26 percent.

Turning to international affairs, Saudi Arabia and Syria signed a bilateral defense cooperation deal on Wednesday. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh for the signing. This was their second meeting in Saudi Arabia in less than a month. The two countries provided no details on what the defense agreement entails. The Saudi Fund for Development also signed six agreements with Syria's Finance Ministry. Those deals provide development loans worth over 403 million dollars to Syria. The loans will support development and service sectors, according to Syria's Finance Ministry. Reuters previously reported that Syria was weighing military assistance to Saudi Arabia.

In economic news, Indonesia's economy grew by 5.47 percent during the third quarter. That rate beat the 5.18 percent growth forecast from a Reuters poll. The country's economy had grown by 5.29 percent in the second quarter. Indonesia is the largest economy in Southeast Asia. Manufacturing supported the growth, including processing palm oil into fuel for biodiesel programs. The state budget projects 5.4 percent economic growth for 2026. Finance minister Suahasil Nazara said growth could reach 5.5 percent this year. Bank Indonesia expects growth between 4.9 percent and 5.7 percent. President Prabowo Subianto aims to reach 8 percent growth by 2029.

Next, looking at business, major global companies are continuing to cut jobs in 2026. Amazon announced in January that it will eliminate around 16,000 corporate roles globally. That move followed an earlier cut of 14,000 roles in October 2025. American Express plans to cut 5 percent of its workforce, impacting up to 4,000 employees. Software company Atlassian is cutting about 1,600 jobs, which is 10 percent of its staff. Several companies cited artificial intelligence as a key reason for their workforce reductions. A World Economic Forum survey found 41 percent of companies expect AI-driven workforce cuts. Barclays, the British financial institution, also plans to cut around 5 percent of its workforce.

Turning to technology, five global banks have established a new non-profit organization in Singapore. The group is called the Global Layer One Organisation, or GL1 Org. The members are HSBC, Kinexys by JPMorgan, MUFG, Societe Generale-Forge, and Standard Chartered. This group aims to build common infrastructure standards for tokenized financial markets. The initiative builds on work started by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. That project explored shared ledger systems for financial institutions to deploy tokenized assets. It also created controls to help institutions embed regulatory rules into digital infrastructure. GL1 Org is now inviting participation from other financial institutions, fintechs, and global policymakers.

In climate news, representatives from over 190 countries will gather for the COP31 UN climate summit. The annual conference will take place in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to November 20. Scientists confirmed this year that the world is on track to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming. Turkey will host the summit, while Australia leads negotiations alongside Pacific Island nations. The Paris Agreement in 2015 committed countries to limit global warming below 2 degrees Celsius. UN Special Adviser Selwin Hart said the main challenge is making clean energy affordable for everyone. Major unresolved issues include how wealthier nations will deliver promised climate finance to developing countries.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Betting apps frequently offer risk-free promotional deals and bonus credits to users. Companies are not actually trying to win back that promo money on your first wager. Placing a free fifty-dollar bet recalibrates your personal baseline. Once you get used to the rush of a large payout, smaller wagers feel less exciting. Your normal five-dollar bets suddenly feel too small to be fun. When free credits run out, you keep placing larger bets with your own bank account. The casino willingly loses a small bonus to permanently upgrade your risk tolerance. Free money is not a gift, but a recalibration. The next time you see a free offer, will you reconsider what it really costs you?

Thank you for listening to the Sift Daily Briefing, and stay informed wherever you go.
